content:
The late Princess Diana's youngest brother, Charles Spencer, has alleged in a new book that King Charles claimed the public would soon forget her after her death in 1997, according to reports about his forthcoming memoir.

According to extracts from the book 'Swan Song: My Sister Diana', first published by the Daily Mail on Wednesday, Spencer claimed he had a heated phone argument with the now-King over whether Princes William and Harry should walk together in their mother's funeral procession.

Writing in the new book, due out next week, Spencer said: 'Prince Charles went on and on, ranting away, and I didn't interrupt him. Then he stopped.'

He added: 'I thought that pause meant he was trying to pull himself together, but then he erupted into what I now recognise as long-suppressed views about Diana, and about her devastating impact on his life and his fear of how the world would react to her death. 'Don't worry,' he said through gritted teeth. 'We'll soon forget her!'"

Spencer wrote that the comments left him "stunned", and that it took him several seconds to respond.

He wrote in the book: "I said quietly, 'I can't believe you just said that.' Then I put the phone down."

Four sample copies of Spencer's new book were stolen from a lorry in the Netherlands, and Dutch authorities are investigating the burglary, the Daily Mail reported on Tuesday.

A publishing source described the theft as "extremely suspicious", and told the paper: "This is unprecedented."

The source told the Mail: "This will very likely be the most important publication of the year, and the security around it has been incredibly tight."

Spencer's spokesperson did not immediately respond to HuffPost's request for comment.

A Buckingham Palace spokesperson, in a statement responding to HuffPost, said: "While we would not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty understands the bond between siblings can be painfully tested by grief, and that judgment can be clouded, and memories shaped, in ways that others may not appreciate."

Spencer delivered a eulogy at Diana's funeral at Westminster Abbey, in which he memorably criticised the British tabloids' relentless pursuit of her story and described his sister as "the most hunted person of the modern age".

Spencer said in a recent social media post that the new book was "the most personal of the ten books I've written in the last thirty years".

He wrote: "It is essentially a simple offering from a brother to an extraordinary sister."

Carly Ledbetter contributed to this report.
